patent: Filed 1992-09-15 (French priority 1991-09-18) and issued 1994-12-20 to Michel Bruel of the French Commissariat à l'Energie Atomique (CEA), where the work was done at its LETI laboratory in Grenoble. It is the basic patent of the process later named Smart Cut. Hydrogen implanted into a donor wafer collects as a thin buried layer of microbubbles near the ion range; the implanted face is joined to a stiffener, and annealing splits the wafer along the bubble layer, so a crystalline film whose thickness is set by the implant energy is transferred onto the stiffener. Compared with the routes it lists, it needs no foreign substrate (silicon on sapphire), no very high oxygen dose (SIMOX) and no doped etch stop (bonded and thinned wafers). Bruel published the process as "Silicon on insulator material technology" (Electronics Letters, vol. 31, no. 14, 1995). It became the main method for making silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafers, licensed to Soitec, a CEA-Leti spin-off founded in 1992, and through Soitec to other wafer makers. The donor wafer left behind can be repolished and reused, which the patent does not discuss. The same implant-and-split transfer is used for other thin crystalline films, among them thin-film lithium niobate on insulator.

figs.1: Implanted hydrogen concentration C against depth P below the implanted face, with no scales. The profile is skewed: a long low tail toward the surface, a sharp peak at Rp (dashed line) and a steep fall beyond it. The microbubble layer of FIGS. 2-3 forms around this peak, so Rp fixes where the wafer later splits.
figs.2: Section through donor wafer 1 during implantation. Arrows 2 are the ion beam entering through face 4; the dash-dot line just above the face is the optional encapsulating layer 10. The dotted band is microbubble layer 3, which divides the wafer into film 5 above and substrate mass 6 below. The paired short strokes are sparse section shading for the crystal; the dash-dot break marks across both side edges show the wafer is drawn broken, so the film is shown far thicker relative to the substrate than it is. The front page repeats this figure without its label.
figs.3: The same wafer with stiffener 7 laid on face 4 over its full width, before the heat treatment: bubble layer 3 is still intact and film 5 still joined to mass 6. The stiffener is drawn as an unshaded box with diagonals, and its material is left open; layer 10 is not drawn here.
figs.4: After the heat treatment: the wafer has split along the former bubble layer, leaving film 5 attached to stiffener 7 and separated by gap 8 from substrate mass 6, whose break marks remain. The gap is drawn much wider than to scale. The front page repeats this figure without its label.

parts.7: Its role in the text is mechanical: pressed or bonded against the face, it holds the surface flat against the gas pressure in the growing bubbles, so the film comes away whole instead of blistering. For SOI the text names a silicon wafer covered with a dielectric layer; in later practice the two wafers are joined by direct wafer bonding.
parts.Rp: Printed as Rp in the drawing and text; the projected range of the implanted ions.

glossary.def: A thin crystalline silicon layer on an insulating layer, usually a buried oxide on a silicon handle wafer. Devices built in the top layer are isolated from the substrate.
The trade name later given to the process of this patent: light-ion implantation, bonding to a second wafer, and splitting by annealing.
Shooting ions of chosen energy into a solid; they come to rest over a spread of depths around a mean depth set by the energy. The dose is the number of ions per unit area (cm^{-2}).
The mean depth below the surface at which implanted ions come to rest; the peak of the concentration profile.

The patent's translation of electronic and nuclear stopping: a fast ion loses energy mostly by exciting electrons, which leaves the lattice intact, and only near the end of its path by knocking atoms out of place.

Nanometre-scale gas-filled cavities formed when implanted hydrogen or rare-gas atoms collect in the crystal. On heating they grow and merge, and their gas pressure cracks the crystal along their plane.
A dome raised on a free surface by gas pressure in a cavity just beneath it; without a stiffener, the implanted surface blisters and flakes instead of separating as a continuous film.
A crystal plane along which the crystal splits easily.
The rigid body held against the implanted face; in SOI manufacture, the handle wafer.
Joining two flat, clean wafer surfaces by contact, without adhesive, then strengthening the bond by heating.
A layer on the wafer surface that the ions pass through; here it reduces ion penetration, protects against contamination or sets the surface state.
Growing a crystalline film on a crystalline substrate of a different material, such as silicon on sapphire.
Separation by implantation of oxygen: a high oxygen dose implanted into silicon and annealed forms a buried oxide layer under a thin silicon film.
A layer, here made by doping, that a chemical etch does not attack, so thinning a wafer stops at a defined depth.
Zone-melting recrystallization: a polycrystalline film on an insulator is melted in a moving narrow zone and regrows with large grains.
A low-index lattice plane such as (100); the patent's "1,0,0 plane".
Kiloelectronvolt, the energy unit for implanted ions; one H^{+} ion accelerated through 150 kV has 150 keV.
